input.question: If our atmosphere was 78% Oxygen instead of nitrogen, would we be able to hold our breath longer?
input.ground_truth: If we hadn't been killed off by fires raging across continents every time there was a lightning storm, or exterminated by gigantic insects, sure. P.S. Insects are limited in size by their relatively inefficient pulmonary systems (and, possibly, their exoskeletons).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If our atmosphere was 78% Oxygen instead of nitrogen, would we be able to hold our breath longer?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the air around us is like a big jar of jelly beans. Right now, most of the jelly beans are one color (nitrogen), and only a few are red (oxygen), which we need to breathe.

But if the jar had mostly red jelly beans (oxygen) instead of the other color, here’s what would happen:

When you hold your breath, your body is using up the red jelly beans (oxygen) inside you. If the air outside has lots and lots of red jelly beans, it might sound like you could hold your breath longer, right? But actually, your body can only use the red jelly beans that are inside you, not the ones outside.

So, having more oxygen in the air around us doesn’t help us hold our breath longer. It just means there’s more oxygen outside, but your lungs can only hold so much, and your body still uses up the oxygen inside you at the same speed.

So, the answer is: **No, we wouldn’t be able to hold our breath longer just because the air has more oxygen.**
